job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — Per-vessel threshold permits fleet splitting.** The 10,000-metric-ton threshold applies to “a single vessel,” allowing an operator to divide recovery among several vessels and keep each below the threshold.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Exactly 10,000 tons is not prohibited.** Because the definition requires “more than 10,000” metric tons, a vessel recovering exactly 10,000 tons in a year falls outside it.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Per year” is undefined.** The bill does not specify calendar year, fiscal year, license year, or a rolling 12-month period, permitting strategic timing and creating disputes over when quantities must be aggregated.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — The prohibition may not attach until the threshold is crossed.** It is unclear whether recovery becomes unlawful only on the day a vessel exceeds 10,000 tons or whether all its mining during that year retroactively qualifies, complicating daily penalties and advance enforcement.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — Recovery can be attributed away from a vessel.** “Recovery … by a single vessel” is undefined where minerals are collected by remotely operated equipment, transferred between vessels, or lifted to a platform rather than directly by the vessel.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — Depth measurement is unspecified.** The bill does not say whether “depths greater than 200 meters” means water depth, depth below sea level, or another measure, nor how operations spanning both sides of the boundary are treated.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — Core terms are undefined.** “Recovery,” “seabed,” and “mineral resources” lack definitions, leaving uncertainty about sampling, dredging, test mining, extraction from the subsoil, and recovery of material already displaced.

8. **Section 2(1)(B) — “The Secretary” is never identified.** The bill assigns potentially prohibition-triggering determinations to an unspecified Cabinet secretary, making the provision difficult to administer and vulnerable to challenge.

9. **Section 2(1)(B) — No standard or procedure governs comparable-risk findings.** “Risks … comparable” is not defined, and the bill supplies no required evidence, rulemaking procedure, notice, hearing, or judicial-review framework. That uncertainty is especially consequential because the finding can support criminal liability.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — The effect and timing of a determination are unclear.** The bill does not say whether a determination applies only prospectively, to a class of activities, or to an individual operation, raising fair-notice and retroactivity problems.

11. **Section 2(2) — The “U.S. person” definition omits many people and entities.** It does not expressly cover U.S. nationals who are not citizens, permanent residents, partnerships, unincorporated associations, trusts, federally chartered entities, or potentially entities formed under tribal or territorial law.

12. **Section 2(2) — Foreign subsidiaries provide an avoidance route.** A foreign-organized subsidiary is not itself a “U.S. person,” even if wholly owned or controlled by a U.S. company; the act also contains no beneficial-ownership, control, direction, or anti-evasion rule.

13. **Section 2(3) — Smaller vessels escape the registry.** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less need not register even though they can conduct prohibited mining, and operators could structure fleets around that cutoff.

14. **Section 2(3) — Exactly 5,000 gross tons is excluded.** “More than 5,000” leaves a vessel measured at precisely 5,000 gross tons outside the definition.

15. **Section 2(3) — “Equipped for” is uncertain and avoidable.** Operators might use modular, removable, leased, or support equipment and argue that a vessel itself is not equipped for recovery. The act also does not specify which gross-tonnage measurement system applies.

16. **Section 3(a) — “Engage in” leaves ancillary conduct uncertain.** The bill does not say whether financing, insuring, directing, processing, purchasing, transporting, brokering, or providing equipment for mining counts as engaging in it, allowing companies to remain involved without directly recovering minerals.

17. **Section 3(a) — Geographic coverage is incomplete and unclear.** Foreign persons acting wholly outside the United States are not covered, while “in the United States” is not defined to address territories, U.S.-flagged ships, the exclusive economic zone, or conduct partly inside and partly outside the country.

18. **Section 3(b) — The exploration-license exemption has no specified issuer.** An operator could argue that a license from any domestic or foreign government—or an international body—qualifies because the provision does not identify an issuing authority.

19. **Section 3(b) — Exploration licenses can become broad mining exemptions.** The provision exempts “mining conducted under” an exploration license, without limiting the exemption to exploration-scale activity, licensed quantities, named vessels, or the license’s original terms.

20. **Section 3(b) — Grandfathering has no expiration or anti-transfer rule.** The bill does not require a pre-enactment license to remain valid, active, or unmodified, and does not address renewals, assignments, ownership changes, expansions, or dormant licenses.

21. **Section 3(b) — The enactment-date cutoff invites a licensing rush.** Licenses issued at any point before presidential signature qualify, even after congressional consideration has made the exemption apparent.

22. **Section 3(c) — The environmental-assessment exemption is purpose-based and uncapped.** An operator can characterize an operation as being conducted “for the purpose” of assessment; there are no quantity, duration, method, approval, scientific-protocol, or independent-verification limits.

23. **Section 3(c) — Mixed-purpose activities are unresolved.** The bill does not say whether environmental assessment must be the sole, primary, or merely one purpose, potentially exempting commercial activity that also collects environmental data.

24. **Section 4(a) — The registry’s jurisdiction and deadline are unspecified.** Read literally, it directs the operator of “each” covered vessel worldwide to register, regardless of U.S. connection, but gives operators no deadline or process for registration.

25. **Section 4 — “Operator” is undefined.** Ownership, chartering, technical management, and operational control may rest with different entities, allowing each to dispute responsibility for registration and reporting.

26. **Section 4(b) — Reporting requirements are too vague for consistent enforcement.** “Describing the recovery activities” establishes no required data fields, locations, quantities, methods, supporting records, or retention period, and does not require reports about vessels claiming no recovery.

27. **Sections 4 and 5 — Registry violations carry no stated penalty.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3, so failure to register, failure to report, and inaccurate or incomplete reports are not violations subject to the act’s civil or criminal penalties.

28. **Section 4 — NOAA receives information but gets no verification powers.** The act provides no inspection, tracking, audit, subpoena, sampling, boarding, or records-access authority, and does not require public disclosure or information-sharing with enforcement agencies.

29. **Section 5(a) — No civil-enforcement mechanism is supplied.** The bill does not identify who assesses or sues for the penalty, what procedures apply, where actions may be brought, or whether injunctions and administrative orders are available.

30. **Section 5(a) — “Each day” is ambiguous.** The bill does not explain whether penalties accrue per vessel, per mining site, per corporate entity, or per continuing course of conduct, or how days are counted for intermittent or threshold-crossing operations.

31. **Section 5 — The remedies may leave violations profitable.** There is no disgorgement, forfeiture, permit revocation, mineral seizure, remediation requirement, or enhanced penalty tied to the value recovered or environmental damage.

32. **Section 5(b) — “Willfully” creates a demanding criminal case.** Prosecutors may have to prove the defendant knew the conduct was unlawful, a significant obstacle given the act’s undefined terms, quantitative threshold, exemptions, and Secretary-dependent category.

33. **Sections 5 and 8 — The penalty and effective-date clauses conflict.** Section 5(a) refers to violations “on or after the date of enactment,” but section 8 says the act does not take effect until 180 days later. That creates uncertainty about whether any duties or liabilities exist during the intervening period.

34. **Section 6 — The international mandate is largely precatory.** “Shall seek to negotiate” requires an effort, not a completed or effective agreement, and the bill supplies no negotiating benchmarks, reporting requirement, consequence for failure, or mechanism for bringing an agreement into force.

35. **Section 6 — “Equivalent” prohibitions could reproduce the bill’s exceptions.** Because equivalence is measured against section 3, an agreement could include the same broad exploration-license and environmental-assessment exemptions rather than a comprehensive international ban.

36. **Section 7(a) — The National Academies report is not actually required.** The act specifies no deadline, commissioning authority, funding, methodology, or criteria for the report on which Congress is supposed to act.

37. **Section 7(a) — “Without serious harm” is undefined.** The standard does not specify the ecosystems, probability, duration, geographic scale, or reversibility of harm, leaving substantial room for competing interpretations.

38. **Section 7(a) — The joint-resolution mechanism is incomplete.** There is no expedited procedure, required statutory text, committee deadline, or explanation of whether the resolution must become law; “Congress … finds” may also obscure the President’s constitutional role in enacting a joint resolution.

39. **Section 7 — The ten-year sunset overrides the ostensibly science-based duration.** Regardless of whether the National Academies issues a report or Congress finds mining safe, the entire act disappears after ten years, allowing mining to resume automatically.

40. **Section 7(b) — Sunset of the entire act creates collateral gaps.** It terminates not only the prohibition but also the registry, reporting system, international-negotiation provision, and express penalty framework; the bill does not state how pending investigations, cases, or retained records should be handled.

41. **Act-wide — No lead implementing or enforcement agency is designated.** NOAA receives registrations, an unidentified Secretary makes risk determinations, and the State Department negotiates internationally, but no official is expressly responsible for regulations, compliance monitoring, or enforcement coordination.

42. **Act-wide — No implementing-rule authority or deadline is provided.** The act depends on unresolved technical and procedural questions but neither expressly authorizes regulations nor requires them before the prohibition takes effect.

43. **Act-wide — There is no express anti-circumvention rule.** Fleet splitting, corporate restructuring, foreign subsidiaries, vessel reflagging, equipment leasing, transshipment, and nominally scientific operations are not expressly addressed.

44. **Act-wide — There is no severability clause.** If a court invalidated a central provision—particularly the vague Secretary-determination mechanism or an application carrying criminal consequences—the absence of a severability instruction could broaden litigation over how much of the act should remain operative.
